summary: Describes the Direct Data Placement protocol, which carries information that allows incoming data to be placed directly in an upper layer's receive buffer. It reduces CPU and memory use. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: DDP tells a receiver where each incoming piece of data belongs, so it can place data directly in an upper-layer buffer. It can place pieces out of order but reports complete messages in order.

questions: what is an stag in ddp
what is the difference between tagged and untagged buffers
how does ddp avoid copying data
subtitle: DDP places received data in its final upper-layer buffer without an intermediate copy.

tldr.problem: Copying received data from an intermediate buffer to its final buffer uses memory bandwidth and CPU time. It also limits throughput to the CPU's copying speed.
tldr.mechanism: Each DDP segment identifies its destination using either a steering tag and offset or a queue number, message sequence number, and offset. Placement can occur out of order, while delivery to the upper layer remains ordered.
tldr.outcome: DDP supports direct placement with tagged and untagged buffers as part of the iWARP protocol family. RFC 5041 has been updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5041 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. It has been updated by RFC 7146 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What Direct Data Placement Does
sections.content:
Direct Data Placement (DDP) carries information that lets a receiver place incoming data directly into an upper-layer protocol's buffer. The receiver does not first copy it through an intermediate buffer. The RFC says this can reduce memory bandwidth and CPU use.

DDP preserves message boundaries and provides two buffer models. It separates placement, which may happen out of order, from delivery, which tells the upper layer that a complete message is ready and must happen in order.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP directs incoming data to its final buffer instead of making an extra copy. The upper layer receives a message only after its pieces are placed and earlier messages are delivered.

sections.title: DDP Between the Transport and Application
sections.content:
DDP sits below an Upper Layer Protocol (ULP) and above a Lower Layer Protocol (LLP). The RFC describes DDP with Marker PDU Aligned Framing over TCP and with an SCTP adaptation. DDP is designed to work with Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP); DDP, RDMAP, and MPA form the iWARP suite.

Each DDP stream maps to one LLP stream. The LLP must provide reliable, in-order delivery within that stream. DDP does not guarantee ordering between separate DDP streams.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP is a layer between a reliable transport and the application protocol. Each DDP stream uses one lower-layer stream, and separate DDP streams have no ordering guarantee between them.

sections.title: What the Lower Layer Must Provide
sections.content:
An LLP used with DDP must expose its maximum record size and changes to that size. It must reliably deliver accepted segments or report failure, preserve segment and message boundaries, and provide each received segment's length. It must also supply a strong digest covering at least the DDP segment, at least equivalent to CRC32-C.

An LLP may provide segments out of order for placement, but it must identify their sender-specified order. It must also report graceful stream and connection teardown and prevent duplicates from being passed to DDP after prior ordered segments have been passed.
sections.plainLanguage: The lower layer must deliver segments reliably, preserve their boundaries, report their size, and provide a strong error check. If it delivers pieces out of order, it must also give their correct order.

sections.title: The Tagged and Untagged Headers
sections.content:
Every DDP segment begins with an 8-bit control field. T selects tagged or untagged placement; L marks the final segment of a message; four reserved bits are zero when sent; and the two-bit DDP version field is 1.

A tagged header adds an STag naming a buffer and a 64-bit Tagged Offset locating the data within it. An untagged header adds a Queue Number, a Message Sequence Number, and a Message Offset. The queue and message number identify the queued buffer; the offset marks the data position in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: A tagged header names a buffer and position. An untagged header names a receive queue, a message number, and a position within that message.

sections.title: Placing and Delivering Messages
sections.content:
The tagged model lets the sender choose a previously advertised buffer and an offset within it. The untagged model uses the next buffer queued by the receiver; a message starts at offset zero, and a message larger than its buffer is an error. DDP divides each message into segments that fit the lower layer's maximum record size.

The receiver may place segments out of order or more than once, but it must deliver each message at most once and in send order. It delivers a message after its final segment arrives, all its segments are placed, and all earlier messages are placed and delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender divides a message into pieces that fit the transport. The receiver can place pieces as they arrive, but it reports each whole message once and in the order sent.

sections.title: Stream Teardown and Receive Errors
sections.content:
DDP does not start stream teardown on its own. It responds to a request from the upper or lower layer. Before placing a non-empty segment, the receiver checks its buffer identifier, queue or message number, offset, and bounds. For tagged placement, it also checks that the offset-plus-length does not wrap.

If a check fails, DDP stops placing the segment, reports the error to the upper layer, and silently drops later incoming segments. It should allow the upper layer to send one further message before the stream ends, so the peer can receive an error indication.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks every destination and position before writing data. If a segment points outside an allowed buffer or has an invalid label, DDP reports an error and drops later incoming pieces.

sections.title: Protecting Memory and DDP Streams
sections.content:
A forged DDP segment could try to write data to a receiver's memory. The receiver must validate the steering tag and exact byte range before placing any data. A steering tag must be associated with its allowed DDP stream or protection domain, and the upper layer controls when its access range is valid or revoked.

DDP does not authenticate the lower-layer stream itself; the upper-layer protocol is responsible for validating it. Where impersonation or stream hijacking is possible, the RFC strongly recommends authentication, integrity, and replay protection. IPsec is one available protection method.
sections.plainLanguage: A false segment could target the wrong part of memory. The receiver checks its tag and range, while the upper-layer protocol is responsible for trusting the connection.
